title: Uganda Independence from Britain
description: Uganda gained independence from British colonial rule on October 9, 1962, with Milton Obote of the Uganda People's Congress becoming the first Prime Minister and the Kabaka of Buganda, Edward Mutesa II, serving as ceremonial President. The independence settlement preserved the federal status of Buganda kingdom, creating a fragile power-sharing arrangement that would soon unravel.

title: First Post-Independence Elections
description: Uganda held general elections shortly before independence, with Milton Obote's Uganda People's Congress forming a coalition government with the Buganda-based Kabaka Yekka party to secure a parliamentary majority. The coalition masked deep tensions between Obote's centralizing ambitions and Buganda's desire for federal autonomy that would define the decade.

title: Uganda Joins the Commonwealth and UN
description: The newly independent Uganda joined the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations, establishing its place in the international order under Prime Minister Obote's non-aligned foreign policy orientation. Uganda also became a founding member of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) in 1963.

title: Mutiny of Ugandan Army Over Pay
description: The Uganda Rifles mutinied at Jinja barracks in January 1964, demanding higher pay and faster Africanization of the officer corps, joining similar mutinies in Kenya and Tanzania. Obote requested British military assistance to suppress the mutiny, restoring order but exposing the fragility of postcolonial military institutions.

title: Gold Smuggling Scandal Rocks Obote Government
description: A parliamentary committee found that Prime Minister Obote and Minister of Defense Idi Amin had illegally smuggled gold and ivory from the Democratic Republic of Congo, implicating senior government figures in corruption. Obote suspended parliament rather than face the motion of no-confidence, beginning an authoritarian turn.

title: Obote Suspends Constitution and Attacks Kabaka's Palace
description: Prime Minister Obote suspended the constitution in February 1966 and assumed executive powers before ordering the army, under Idi Amin, to storm the Kabaka's palace at Mengo in May 1966. The Kabaka Edward Mutesa II fled into exile in Britain, and the kingdoms of Buganda and other traditional states were abolished, ending the federal compromise of independence.

title: Pigeon-Hole Constitution Centralizes Power
description: Obote introduced a new republican constitution in 1967 that abolished all traditional kingdoms and established a unitary republic with an executive presidency, known derisively as the 'Pigeon-Hole Constitution' because MPs were reportedly given no time to read it before voting. The constitution concentrated power in the presidency and eliminated the federal protections that had underwritten Buganda's cooperation with independence.

title: Assassination Attempt on Obote
description: An assassination attempt on President Obote at an UPC rally in December 1969 wounded him in the jaw, triggering a severe political crackdown including the banning of opposition parties and detention of political opponents. The incident accelerated Uganda's slide toward one-party rule and intensified Obote's reliance on the military.

title: Idi Amin Military Coup
description: General Idi Amin Dada seized power on January 25, 1971 while President Obote was abroad at a Commonwealth summit in Singapore, in a military coup backed by units loyal to him. Amin initially received broad popular support including from Buganda and Western powers who welcomed the removal of the left-leaning Obote, but his regime quickly descended into one of Africa's most brutal dictatorships.

title: Amin's Massacre of Acholi and Langi Soldiers
description: Within weeks of seizing power, Idi Amin ordered the systematic murder of Acholi and Langi soldiers who formed the backbone of Obote's loyal military units, with thousands killed in barrack massacres across the country. The killings eliminated a potential military challenge to Amin's rule and began the ethnic targeting that characterized his entire regime.

title: Expulsion of Ugandan Asians
description: On August 4, 1972, Idi Amin announced that approximately 80,000 Ugandan Asians of South Asian descent would be expelled within 90 days, claiming a divine vision instructed him to do so and accusing the community of economic exploitation. The expulsion devastated Uganda's economy as the Asian community had owned most of the country's businesses, shops, and professional services, triggering an economic collapse from which Uganda would not recover for over a decade.

title: Economic Nationalization Following Asian Expulsion
description: Amin transferred approximately 5,655 Asian-owned businesses, farms, and properties to Ugandan citizens — primarily his military cronies — under a program called 'economic war.' The new owners lacked business experience and many enterprises quickly failed, collapsing Uganda's commercial sector and causing severe shortages of consumer goods and essential imports.

title: Diplomatic Rupture with Britain and Israel
description: Amin expelled Israeli military advisers in 1972 and severed diplomatic relations with Israel after Israel declined to supply jet fighters, pivoting instead to Libya and Palestinian support. He also broke relations with Britain over the expulsion of British Asians, aligning Uganda with the Arab bloc and becoming a leading voice in the OAU against Israel.

title: Reign of Terror — State Research Bureau Killings
description: Amin's dreaded State Research Bureau (SRB) and Public Safety Unit conducted widespread extrajudicial killings, torture, and disappearances, with victims including politicians, lawyers, doctors, academics, and military officers perceived as threats. Historians estimate between 100,000 and 500,000 Ugandans were killed during Amin's rule from 1971 to 1979, with the worst period concentrated in 1972-76.

title: Amin Declares Uganda an Islamic Republic
description: Amin, a Muslim, declared Uganda an Islamic state and sought financial support from Libya's Muammar Gaddafi and Saudi Arabia, introducing Islamic holidays and cultivating ties with the Arab world. While Uganda's population was predominantly Christian, Amin distributed political and military positions disproportionately to Muslims and members of his Kakwa ethnic group.

title: Entebbe Hostage Crisis
description: Palestinian and German militant hijackers diverted an Air France flight to Entebbe airport in June 1976, taking over 100 Jewish and Israeli hostages with Amin's cooperation and using Uganda as their base of operations. Israel's elite Sayeret Matkal unit carried out a spectacular rescue operation on July 4, 1976, freeing all but three hostages in a raid that humiliated Amin and became one of the most celebrated counter-terrorism operations in history.

title: Murder of Archbishop Janani Luwum
description: Anglican Archbishop of Uganda Janani Luwum was arrested in February 1977 after publicly protesting Amin's human rights abuses, then found dead — officially described as killed in a car accident but widely understood to have been murdered on Amin's orders. His death shocked the international community and the Anglican Communion, intensifying international condemnation of the Amin regime.

title: Uganda Invades Tanzania — Kagera Salient
description: Amin's forces invaded the Kagera region of Tanzania in October 1978, annexing approximately 1,800 square kilometers of Tanzanian territory north of the Kagera River in what appeared to be an attempt to distract from domestic crises. President Julius Nyerere of Tanzania refused Amin's claims and organized a counter-offensive that would ultimately end Amin's rule.

title: Tanzania-Uganda War — Amin Overthrown
description: Tanzanian forces, joined by Ugandan exiles organized as the Uganda National Liberation Army, launched a full-scale counter-invasion in January 1979 and captured Kampala on April 11, 1979, ending Idi Amin's eight-year rule. Amin fled to Libya and later Saudi Arabia, where he lived in comfortable exile until his death in 2003, never facing justice for the estimated 300,000 killed under his regime.

title: Post-Amin Transitional Governments
description: After Amin's fall, Uganda experienced a succession of transitional governments — Yusuf Lule, then Godfrey Binaisa — as the Uganda National Liberation Front struggled to establish stable governance amid competing military factions and the withdrawal of Tanzanian troops. The transitional period was characterized by continued violence, looting, and political fragmentation.

title: Controversial Elections Return Obote to Power
description: Presidential and parliamentary elections held in December 1980 were widely condemned as fraudulent, with Milton Obote declared the winner in a vote that Yoweri Museveni's Uganda Patriotic Movement and international observers alleged was rigged by the Uganda National Liberation Army military faction loyal to Obote. The disputed result directly triggered the Bush War insurgency.

title: Bush War Begins — Museveni's NRA Insurgency
description: Yoweri Museveni launched a guerrilla insurgency from the Luwero Triangle region north of Kampala in February 1981, after alleging the 1980 elections were stolen, with his National Resistance Army (NRA) beginning operations with 27 fighters armed with a handful of weapons from a government armory raid. The five-year Bush War would kill an estimated 500,000 civilians and transform Museveni into Uganda's dominant political figure.

title: Luwero Triangle Massacres
description: Obote's army conducted widespread massacres and forced displacement of civilians in the Luwero Triangle in an effort to deny support to Museveni's NRA guerrillas, with skulls and bones left in the open later becoming symbols of the atrocities. Human rights organizations documented tens of thousands of civilian deaths in the Luwero area between 1981 and 1985.

title: Okello Coup Deposes Obote
description: Acholi military officers led by General Tito Okello staged a coup against Milton Obote in July 1985, deposing him and establishing a military council government. The coup reflected the collapse of Obote's authority after years of counter-insurgency failure, but Okello's government lasted only months before Museveni's NRA captured Kampala.

title: Museveni and NRA Capture Kampala
description: Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army captured Kampala on January 26, 1986 after a rapid military advance, ending the civil war and bringing to power a new government that presented itself as a broad-based administration committed to ending the cycles of ethnic and military politics that had plagued Uganda since independence. Museveni was sworn in as president, beginning what would become Africa's longest-running incumbency.

title: Truth Commission on Human Rights Violations
description: The new Museveni government established the Commission of Inquiry into Violations of Human Rights to investigate abuses from independence through 1986, documenting the full scope of atrocities under Amin and Obote. The commission reported extensively but few perpetrators faced justice, establishing a pattern of transitional justice without accountability.

title: Northern Uganda Insurgency Erupts
description: Following Museveni's victory, defeated Acholi soldiers fled north and regrouped under various insurgent groups including the Uganda People's Democratic Army, beginning a cycle of northern insurgency that would persist for two decades. The north-south divide, rooted in colonial-era patterns of recruitment and now deepened by civil war grievances, became Uganda's most persistent political and security fracture.

title: Lord's Resistance Army Founded by Joseph Kony
description: Joseph Kony emerged as leader of what became the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) in northern Uganda in 1987-88, originally inspired by Alice Lakwena's Holy Spirit Movement and claiming a divine mission to rule Uganda according to the Ten Commandments. The LRA would become one of the world's most brutal insurgent groups, abducting an estimated 66,000 children to use as soldiers and sex slaves over the following two decades.

title: Economic Liberalization Under IMF Structural Adjustment
description: Uganda adopted an IMF-supported structural adjustment program in 1987-88, liberalizing the economy, removing price controls, and devaluing the currency after years of economic collapse under Amin and Obote. The reforms produced one of Africa's strongest growth records through the 1990s and reduced poverty significantly, becoming a showcase for market-oriented development on the continent.

title: Uganda Pioneers HIV/AIDS Response
description: Uganda became internationally celebrated for its aggressive early HIV/AIDS public health campaign under Museveni, achieving one of Africa's first sustained declines in HIV prevalence from approximately 15 percent in the late 1980s to under 8 percent by the mid-1990s through its 'ABC' (Abstain, Be faithful, use Condoms) messaging. The success became a global model for AIDS prevention in high-prevalence settings.

title: Traditional Kingdoms Restored
description: Museveni's government restored the traditional kingdoms of Buganda, Toro, Bunyoro, and Ankole in 1993, reversing Obote's 1967 abolition and reinstating the Kabaka of Buganda Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II in a ceremonial role. The restoration was popular but also a calculated move to win Buganda's political acquiescence, as the kingdoms received no governmental powers under the arrangement.

title: Constituent Assembly Elections
description: Uganda held elections for a Constituent Assembly in March 1994 to debate and adopt a new constitution, with candidates standing as individuals rather than political parties under Museveni's 'movement' system that banned partisan activity. The assembly process was inclusive but the movement system's restrictions on opposition were a major point of controversy.

title: New Constitution Enacted — Movement System Retained
description: Uganda promulgated a new constitution in October 1995 that established a democratic framework with separation of powers and extensive rights protections, but retained the 'movement system' that prohibited political parties from organizing, effectively entrenching Museveni's National Resistance Movement as the only political actor. The constitution was regarded as progressive in structure but the movement system clause kept Uganda short of genuine multiparty democracy.

title: First Presidential Election Under New Constitution
description: Museveni won Uganda's first direct presidential election in May 1996 with approximately 74 percent of the vote, defeating Paul Ssemogerere of the Democratic Party in a contest that international observers considered largely free and fair despite the ban on partisan campaigning. The election legitimized Museveni's rule internationally and marked the beginning of his transformation from liberation leader to entrenched incumbent.

title: Uganda Intervenes in Congo's Civil War
description: Uganda deployed troops into the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1996-97 to support Laurent-Désiré Kabila's overthrow of Mobutu Sese Seko, and subsequently remained in eastern Congo pursuing LRA remnants and securing mineral-rich territory. Uganda's long intervention in eastern Congo generated substantial resource extraction and was later found by the International Court of Justice to have violated international law.

title: LRA Abduction Campaign Intensifies
description: The Lord's Resistance Army intensified mass abductions of children throughout Acholiland in northern Uganda in the late 1990s, with children as young as eight being forced to become soldiers or 'wives' of commanders in practices that constituted war crimes and crimes against humanity. By 1998 approximately 1.6 million civilians in northern Uganda had been displaced into protected camps under government orders that themselves generated severe humanitarian conditions.

title: Rwenzori Mountain Massacre by Allied Democratic Forces
description: The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamist rebel group based in the Rwenzori mountains bordering Congo, attacked Kichwamba Technical College in June 1998 burning dormitories and killing 80 students, one of the deadliest single attacks on civilians in Uganda's post-Amin period. The ADF remained active in eastern Congo for decades, later becoming affiliated with the Islamic State.

title: Referendum Extends Movement-Only System
description: Uganda held a referendum in June 2000 on whether to continue the movement system or return to multiparty politics, producing a 90 percent vote to continue the movement system in a contest that the main opposition parties boycotted as unfair. Donors and democracy advocates criticized the result as entrenching Museveni's hold on power under the guise of popular consultation.

title: Movement for the Restoration of the Ten Commandments Massacre
description: A doomsday cult called the Movement for the Restoration of the Ten Commandments of God burned alive approximately 778 followers in Kanungu district on March 17, 2000 in one of the world's deadliest mass murder-suicides in history, with additional victims found in mass graves at affiliated properties. The massacre shocked Uganda and raised questions about the vulnerability of rural communities to religious exploitation amid decades of trauma.

title: Museveni Re-Elected Amid Opposition Allegations
description: Museveni won the March 2001 presidential election with 69 percent of the vote over Kizza Besigye, his former personal physician and NRM insider who had accused the movement of corruption and personalization of power. The election was marred by violence and intimidation of opposition supporters, and the Supreme Court found irregularities though it declined to annul the result.

title: Operation Iron Fist Against LRA
description: Uganda launched Operation Iron Fist in March 2002, deploying the Uganda People's Defence Force into southern Sudan to attack LRA bases at Juba with Sudanese government permission. The operation failed to eliminate the LRA and provoked a massive retaliatory surge of LRA attacks inside northern Uganda, dramatically worsening the humanitarian crisis in Acholiland.

title: Northern Uganda Humanitarian Crisis Peaks
description: By 2003-2004, approximately 1.7 million internally displaced persons were living in crowded, disease-ridden camps in northern Uganda, described by UN Emergency Relief Coordinator Jan Egeland as the world's largest forgotten humanitarian crisis. Mortality rates in the camps exceeded conflict mortality as cholera, malaria, and malnutrition killed thousands, and children made dangerous nightly commutes to towns to avoid LRA abductions.

title: Barlonyo Massacre by LRA
description: The LRA attacked the Barlonyo internally displaced persons camp in Lira district on February 21, 2004, killing between 200 and 300 civilians sheltering in the camp — one of the single deadliest LRA attacks of the conflict. The massacre occurred despite the camp's proximity to government forces and highlighted the profound failure to protect civilians.

title: Multiparty System Restored by Referendum
description: Uganda's July 2005 referendum voted overwhelmingly to restore multiparty political competition, ending the movement system that had restricted political parties since 1986, following sustained domestic and donor pressure. The same constitutional amendments controversially removed the two-term presidential limit, allowing Museveni to run for a third term in 2006.

title: ICC Indicts LRA Leadership
description: The International Criminal Court issued its first-ever arrest warrants in October 2005, targeting Joseph Kony and four other LRA commanders for crimes against humanity and war crimes including murder, rape, sexual enslavement, and the conscription of child soldiers. The warrants complicated peace negotiations, with Kony demanding their withdrawal as a precondition for signing any peace agreement.

title: Juba Peace Talks with LRA
description: Direct peace negotiations began between the Ugandan government and the LRA in Juba, South Sudan in July 2006 under South Sudanese mediation, resulting in a cessation of hostilities agreement that effectively ended large-scale LRA violence inside Uganda. Kony refused to sign the final peace agreement in April 2008, citing the ICC arrest warrants, but the talks ended the northern Uganda phase of the conflict.

title: Museveni Wins Third Term in First Multiparty Election
description: Museveni won the February 2006 presidential election with 59 percent of the vote against Kizza Besigye in Uganda's first multiparty election since 1980, though the election was held while Besigye faced treason and rape charges widely seen as politically motivated. The EU observer mission found the election fell short of international standards due to intimidation and misuse of state resources.

title: Anti-Homosexuality Bill Introduced
description: MP David Bahati introduced the Anti-Homosexuality Bill in October 2009, originally proposing the death penalty for some homosexual acts and generating intense international condemnation from Western governments and human rights organizations. The bill reflected growing evangelical Christian influence in Ugandan politics and sparked a decade-long struggle over LGBTQ rights that continued through the 2023 law.

title: Kampala Bombings by Al-Shabaab
description: Al-Shabaab detonated bombs at two public venues in Kampala on July 11, 2010 as crowds watched the FIFA World Cup final, killing 76 people in Uganda's deadliest terrorist attack and the first Al-Shabaab attack outside Somalia. Uganda was targeted because of its role as the largest troop contributor to the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM).

title: Walk-to-Work Protests and Crackdown
description: Uganda's main opposition leader Kizza Besigye launched 'Walk-to-Work' protests in April 2011 against rising food and fuel prices following Museveni's disputed re-election, leading to violent security force crackdowns that killed several protesters and left Besigye repeatedly pepper-sprayed and arrested. The protests reflected growing urban economic discontent and galvanized civil society despite the brutal response.

title: Museveni Wins Fourth Presidential Term
description: Museveni won the February 2011 presidential election with 68 percent of the vote in a contest marked by unprecedented campaign spending financed by state resources, substantial vote-buying, and opposition allegations of fraud. The Commonwealth observer mission noted improvements over 2006 while finding continued misuse of incumbency advantages that undermined the level playing field.

title: Invisible Children Kony 2012 Campaign
description: The NGO Invisible Children released the 'Kony 2012' viral video in March 2012, generating over 100 million views in days and bringing global attention to the LRA's atrocities and Joseph Kony's continuing evasion of the ICC arrest warrant. The campaign sparked debate about advocacy, the LRA's diminished size, and the complexity of international engagement with the conflict.

title: Anti-Homosexuality Act Signed into Law
description: President Museveni signed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in February 2014 following years of legislative efforts, imposing life imprisonment for homosexual acts in the most severe anti-LGBTQ legislation outside a handful of countries, though the Constitutional Court annulled it on procedural grounds later in 2014. The episode severely damaged Uganda's international reputation and prompted several donors to redirect aid.

title: Constitutional Court Nullifies Anti-Homosexuality Act
description: Uganda's Constitutional Court struck down the Anti-Homosexuality Act in August 2014 on the procedural grounds that parliament lacked quorum when it passed the bill, a narrow ruling that avoided addressing the substantive rights questions. Activists and observers noted the ruling provided only temporary relief as supporters pledged to reintroduce the legislation through a proper parliamentary process.

title: Museveni Wins Fifth Term Amid Besigye Arrest
description: Museveni was declared the winner of the February 2016 presidential election with 60 percent of the vote while principal challenger Kizza Besigye was repeatedly arrested before, during, and after election day, and placed under house arrest while results were announced. The EU, Commonwealth, and African Union observer missions criticized the election management and the treatment of opposition candidates.

title: Parliament Removes Presidential Age Limit
description: Uganda's parliament voted in December 2017 to remove the constitutional age limit of 75 for presidential candidates, clearing the way for Museveni — then 73 — to run for president indefinitely. The amendment passed amid chaotic scenes in parliament where soldiers entered the chamber and several opposition MPs were forcibly removed and beaten, generating widespread domestic and international condemnation.

title: EACOP Pipeline Agreement Signed
description: Uganda and Tanzania signed agreements with TotalEnergies and CNOOC for the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), a proposed 1,443-kilometer heated pipeline from Uganda's Lake Albert oil fields to the Tanzanian port of Tanga. The project, valued at over $5 billion, faced sustained international pressure from environmental groups, with critics arguing it would displace over 100,000 people and threaten the Lake Victoria ecosystem.

title: Bobi Wine Emerges as Opposition Leader
description: Robert Kyagulanyi, known as Bobi Wine, rose as a major political figure after his 2017 by-election victory, articulating the frustrations of Uganda's large youth population and explicitly challenging Museveni's long incumbency through his 'People Power' movement. Bobi Wine was arrested in August 2018 on treason charges after soldiers were killed near his campaign vehicle in Arua, and was allegedly tortured in military detention.

title: COVID-19 Lockdown and Economic Disruption
description: Uganda imposed one of Africa's strictest COVID-19 lockdowns from March 2020, closing schools, churches, and most businesses for extended periods, with schools ultimately remaining closed for nearly two years — among the longest school closures globally. The lockdown devastated Uganda's informal economy, reversed poverty reduction gains, and disproportionately affected women, youth, and the urban poor.

title: Election Campaign Violence — Bobi Wine Crackdown
description: Security forces killed at least 54 people and arrested thousands during protests that erupted in November 2020 following the arrest of Bobi Wine during the presidential campaign, with Amnesty International documenting arbitrary detentions and torture of opposition supporters. The violence represented the most deadly political crackdown Uganda had seen since the 1980s.

title: Museveni Wins Sixth Term — Bobi Wine Claims Fraud
description: Museveni was declared the winner of the January 14, 2021 presidential election with 58 percent of the vote against Bobi Wine, who claimed massive fraud and said he believed he had won. The election took place under an internet blackout, with observers restricted, and Wine was placed under house arrest for days after the results were announced, unable to communicate with the outside world.

title: Kampala Suicide Bombings
description: Three coordinated suicide bombings struck central Kampala on October 23, 2021, including near parliament and police headquarters, killing at least four people and wounding more than 33 in attacks claimed by the Allied Democratic Forces acting in the name of the Islamic State. The bombings prompted a security crackdown and reignited concerns about domestic radicalization.

title: Oil Production Start — Tilenga Project
description: TotalEnergies began drilling production wells at the Tilenga oil project in the Albertine Rift in 2022, moving toward first oil production from Uganda's estimated 6.5 billion barrel reserves, the largest landlocked discovery in Africa. Civil society groups and the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights raised concerns about displacement of communities in and around Murchison Falls National Park.

title: Uganda Hosts One Million South Sudanese Refugees
description: Uganda maintained its status as Africa's largest refugee-hosting country with over 1.5 million refugees, the vast majority from South Sudan and Democratic Republic of Congo, under Uganda's internationally praised open-door policy that grants refugees freedom of movement and the right to work. The scale of the refugee population strained resources in northern and western Uganda while aid funding fell below emergency response needs.

title: Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 — Among World's Harshest
description: President Museveni signed into law the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 in May 2023, imposing the death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality' and up to life imprisonment for same-sex relations, widely described as among the harshest anti-LGBTQ legislation in the world. The United States suspended Uganda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preferences, and the World Bank paused new public-financing projects in Uganda citing human rights concerns.

title: International Sanctions and Aid Restrictions Over LGBTQ Law
description: Following the Anti-Homosexuality Act, the United States revoked Uganda's AGOA duty-free trade access worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and the World Bank halted new direct lending to the government, while the EU and several bilateral donors reviewed their aid programs. The economic impact was limited in the short term but signaled growing isolation of Uganda's government from major Western partners.

title: Ebola Outbreak Sudan Strain Contained
description: Uganda successfully contained an Ebola outbreak caused by the Sudan strain of the virus, which killed 55 people and infected 142 between September and November 2022, impressing international health authorities with the speed of containment given the absence of an approved vaccine for this strain. The response drew on Uganda's considerable experience managing multiple Ebola outbreaks since 2000.

title: EACOP Construction Advances Amid Protests
description: Construction of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline continued in 2024 despite ongoing international investor pressure, with European banks and insurers declining to finance the project following environmental and human rights concerns raised by dozens of civil society organizations. TotalEnergies proceeded with African and Asian financing partners, setting a target of first oil exports through the pipeline in the late 2020s.

title: Continued Political Repression of Opposition and Media
description: Ugandan authorities continued to arrest opposition politicians, journalists, and civil society activists in 2024, with Bobi Wine's National Unity Platform members reporting systematic harassment and arbitrary detention of supporters. Freedom House classified Uganda as 'Not Free', with particular deterioration in political rights and civil liberties compared to the Museveni government's earlier years.

title: LRA Still Active in Congo Despite Uganda Phase Ending
description: Joseph Kony's Lord's Resistance Army remained active in the Central African Republic and Democratic Republic of Congo in 2024, greatly reduced from its peak but still conducting raids and abductions, with Kony believed to be alive in the CAR-Sudan border area. The ICC warrant for Kony remained outstanding, and one LRA commander — Dominic Ongwen — was serving a 25-year ICC sentence delivered in 2021.

title: Half of Uganda's Banks Face Insolvency in 1994 Banking Crisis
description: By the close of 1994, 60-80% of loans held by Ugandan commercial banks were classified nonperforming and more than half of the country's banking institutions faced insolvency. The crisis was rooted in weak credit assessment and politically directed lending in the years following financial-sector liberalization, and it prompted a wave of license revocations and stricter capital requirements later in the decade. A subsequent 1998-99 crisis saw four more banks holding 12.1% of system deposits closed for insolvency.
